interactions.label: Layout
interactions.teaches: Seeing all three rows at once isolates the changing substitution pattern, while the single-row mode lets the learner test one mirror pair without clutter

interactions.label: Focused compound

demo_steps.title: Source comparison view
demo_steps.narration: The figure begins as three stacked rows: CH3X, CH2XY, and CHXYZ. The formula, wedge drawing, 3D model, mirror, and reflected model repeat across each row so the only changing feature is the number of different groups attached to carbon.

demo_steps.title: CH3X: three identical groups
demo_steps.narration: Focus on CH3X. Because three substituents are identical hydrogens, the mirror image can be rotated into the same arrangement as the original.

demo_steps.title: CH2XY: two identical groups
demo_steps.narration: Focus on CH2XY. The two hydrogens are still interchangeable, so the mirror image is also superimposable on the original tetrahedron.

demo_steps.title: CHXYZ: four different groups
demo_steps.narration: Focus on CHXYZ. Now every substituent is unique, so the mirror image cannot be rotated to place X, H, Y, and Z all on the same positions at once; this is the structural origin of molecular handedness.

demo_steps.title: Return to the full comparison
demo_steps.narration: Returning to the three-row layout makes the pattern clear: CH3X and CH2XY are achiral at carbon, but CHXYZ has a stereogenic carbon and a non-superimposable mirror image.

plan.geometry_notes: Use an axonometric textbook-figure composition with no strong perspective convergence. Overall three-row source layout spans about X = -7.0 to +7.0, Y = -3.2 to +3.2, Z = -0.5 to +1.6. World convention: +X is screen-right, +Y is screen-up, +Z is the shallow receding depth direction. Row centers: CH3X at Y = +2.1, CH2XY at Y = 0.0, CHXYZ at Y = -2.1. Each row places the condensed formula at X ≈ -6.2, structural formula centered at X ≈ -4.0, original ball-and-stick molecule centered at X ≈ -1.2, mirror pane around X ≈ +2.3, and reflected molecule centered at X ≈ +4.7 behind/right of the mirror. Spread columns generously so each reads like the source: formula-to-structure gap about 1.8 units, structure-to-model gap about 2.5 units, model-to-mirror gap about 2.3 units, mirror-to-reflection gap about 2.0 units. Condensed formula text height about 0.34 world units; structural formula text height about 0.28 world units. Mirror pane dimensions: X thickness 0.05, Y height 6.3, Z/depth width 1.15, colored pale blue #cfe7f5 at opacity 0.35, with subtle highlight #f4fbff opacity 0.55 and edge color #2f9ec3. Do not add a prominent 'mirror' label; if any label is needed, keep it very small and muted or omit it by default. Structural drawings are flat screen-facing graphics: central C in black #111111; upper plain bond from C to X vertical/up; right plain bond from C to H or Y; hashed/dashed wedge from C down-left/back to H; solid filled wedge from C down-right/front to H or Z. Use bond lengths about 0.45 units in the structural drawings. Hashed wedge should be 5 to 7 short black strokes expanding away from C, not a single dashed line. Solid wedge should be a filled black triangular wedge. Ball-and-stick scale: central carbon sphere radius 0.18, substituent sphere radius 0.16, bond cylinder radius 0.035, C-to-substituent distance 0.62. Original tetrahedral orientation per row: X/red-orange is above the carbon and slightly backward; the in-plane/right substituent is to the screen-right and slightly back; the hashed-wedge/back substituent is down-left and back; the solid-wedge/front substituent is down-right and toward viewer. Reflected molecules must be true left-right mirror reversals across the vertical mirror plane: if an original substituent appears on the screen-left side of its tetrahedron, its reflected counterpart appears on the screen-right side, while vertical up/down placement remains visually comparable. Substituent identities by row: CH3X has X at the top and H at right, hashed-wedge, and solid-wedge positions; CH2XY has X at top, Y at right, H on hashed wedge, H on solid wedge; CHXYZ has X at top, Y at right, H on hashed wedge, Z on solid wedge. Colors: carbon dark gray #4f555c, X text magenta #ff00a6, X sphere red-orange #c44732, H text and spheres green #18a85a, Y text and sphere cyan-blue #00a6e8, Z text and sphere gold #caa21a, bonds black #111111. In single-row superposition test mode, enlarge the selected row by about 1.25× and center it vertically, while fading the two unselected rows or hiding them; show the mirror-image molecule translated beside the original as a translucent overlay. For CH3X and CH2XY, align same-colored substituent positions exactly in the overlay; for CHXYZ, align carbon and one or two substituents but leave at least one unique colored sphere visibly mismatched.
plan.notes: Default view must reproduce the full three-row textbook composition rather than replacing it with a single selected molecule. Keep interaction controls small and secondary. Render formula and structural drawings as crisp screen-facing text/2D geometry layered into the 3D scene. Use instanced or cloned row templates so equal substituents keep equal size across rows; do not scale sphere size by row order. The mirror should be a simple translucent pane with a subtle highlight only; avoid halos, target rings, oversized labels, strong reflections, or extra explanatory graphics in the default source-layout view. Superposition guides appear only when showSuperposition is true in single-row mode, and should be translucent enough not to distract from the original figure geometry.

authoredPrompt: This figure arranges three generalized carbon compounds in three rows and reflects each one in a drawn mirror. Each row begins at the left with a condensed formula written in colored letters, "CH3X", "CH2XY", and "CHXYZ", with X in magenta, Y in blue, and Z in gold. Next comes a structural drawing in which a central "C" bonds upward by a plain line, to the left and right by plain lines, and downward by a heavy wedge; the four attached labels are X, H, H and H in the top row, X, H, Y and H in the middle row, and X, H, Y and Z in the bottom row. Third in each row is a ball-and-stick model with a dark gray carbon carrying a red sphere above and green, blue, or yellow spheres below according to the substituents named. At the right stands a tall pale blue rectangular pane with a highlight streak, representing a mirror, and behind it each model appears again as its reflection, with the substituent spheres reversed left to right. Repeating the same three columns down every row isolates substitution pattern as the only variable, so the reader can test each reflection against its original. The layout introduces the condition under which a tetrahedral carbon and its mirror image cease to be superimposable, the structural basis of molecular handedness.
authoredInteractions:
- Drag for moving each mirror-image model onto its original; CH3X and CH2XY can be aligned by rotation while CHXYZ leaves mismatched colored substituents, making superimposability the test for chirality.
- Toggle between CH3X, CH2XY, and CHXYZ rows; the mirror pane and color scheme remain fixed while only substituent variety changes, clarifying why four different groups at tetrahedral carbon create handedness.
authoredContext:
What causes molecular handedness? Look at generalized molecules of the type CH3X, CH2XY, and CHXYZ shown in the figure. On the left are three molecules, and on the right are their images reflected in a mirror. The CH3X and CH2XY molecules are identical to their mirror images and thus are not handed. If you make a molecular model of each molecule and its mirror image, you find that you can superimpose one on the other so that all atoms coincide. The CHXYZ molecule, by contrast, is not identical to its mirror image. You can’t superimpose a model of this molecule on a model of its mirror image for the same reason that you can’t superimpose a left hand on a right hand: they simply aren’t the same.

Tetrahedral carbon atoms and their mirror images. Molecules of the type CH3X and CH2XY are identical to their mirror images, but a molecule of the type CHXYZ is not. A CHXYZ molecule is related to its mirror image in the same way a right hand is related to a left hand.

The figure shows condensed formulas, structures, and ball-and-stick models of C H 3 X, C H 2 X Y, and C H X Y Z along with their mirror images.

A molecule that is not identical to its mirror image is a kind of stereoisomer (another section) called an enantiomer (e-nan-tee-oh-mer, from the Greek enantio, meaning “opposite”). Enantiomers are related to each other as a right hand is related to a left hand and result whenever a tetrahedral carbon is bonded to four different substituents (one need not be H). For example, lactic acid (2-hydroxypropanoic acid) exists as a pair of enantiomers because there are four different groups (−H, −OH, −CH3, −CO2H) bonded to the central carbon atom. The enantiomers are called (+)-lactic acid and (−)-lactic acid. Both are found in sour milk, but only the (+) enantiomer occurs in muscle tissue.

interactions.label: Compound
interactions.teaches: Changing only the number of distinct substituent groups shows that tetrahedral handedness appears only when all four groups around carbon are different
Dragging and rotating the reflected molecule onto the original tests superimposability directly: CH3X and CH2XY can be made to match, while CHXYZ keeps one or more colored groups mismatched

demo_steps.title: Three identical H groups
demo_steps.narration: With CH3X, the mirror image looks reversed at first, but the three green H groups are interchangeable. The reflected model can be rotated onto the original so every color matches.

demo_steps.title: Two identical H groups
demo_steps.narration: With CH2XY, there are still two identical green H groups. The mirror image can again be rotated into coincidence with the original, so this carbon is not chiral.

demo_steps.title: Four different groups
demo_steps.narration: With CHXYZ, each substituent has a unique color. When the mirror image is dragged onto the original, one matched orientation always leaves another colored group in the wrong place, revealing non-superimposable mirror images.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Use a single-row version of the source layout. World coordinate convention: +X is screen-right, +Y is screen-up, +Z is the receding diagonal. Overall visible layout spans about X = -5.2 to +4.3, Y = -2.1 to +2.1, Z = -0.6 to +1.8. Condensed formula sits at X ≈ -4.7, Y ≈ 0.15 as flat text; structural formula is centered at X ≈ -3.15; original ball-and-stick model is centered near X ≈ -1.15; mirror pane is centered near X ≈ +2.0 and extends in Y and Z; reflected molecule begins inside/behind the pane near X ≈ +2.25, Z ≈ +0.75. Mirror pane dimensions: about 0.06 × 4.2 × 2.25 world units, where X is thickness, Y is vertical height, and Z is the pane width receding diagonally; color pale blue #cfe7f5 with opacity about 0.45, darker right edge #00779d. Ball-and-stick scale: carbon sphere radius about 0.22, substituent spheres radius about 0.18, bond cylinders radius about 0.035, C-to-substituent distance about 0.82. Tetrahedral bond directions for the original model: X/red-orange points upward and slightly back; one H/green points left; one substituent points right and slightly back; the front/down substituent points down and toward the viewer. Reflected model should be the mirror reflection of the original across the vertical mirror plane, so its left-right substituent order is reversed. Colors: carbon dark gray #596169, X sphere red-orange #b94432 while X text is magenta #ff00a6, H text/spheres green #009b55 to #24b86a, Y text/sphere cyan-blue #00a8e8, Z text/sphere gold #c9a316, structural bonds black #111111. Structural drawing is flat, with central C black, vertical X bond, left H bond, right H/Y bond, and a solid wedge down-right to the front H or Z; the same substituent identities as the ball model must be used for each selected compound.
interactionPlan.notes: Render formula and wedge-bond structure as screen-facing text and line geometry so they remain legible while the 3D molecular models retain depth. The compound toggle should swap only substituent labels and sphere colors/identities, keeping the carbon position, mirror pane, camera, and tetrahedral geometry fixed. The drag interaction should apply a rigid-body transform to the reflected molecule; during dragging, show translucent colored target halos at the original molecule’s substituent positions and mark matching color overlaps green and mismatched overlaps red. For CH3X and CH2XY, allow rotations that demonstrate color-equivalent superposition; for CHXYZ, the best-fit overlay should visibly leave at least one unique substituent color out of place. Keep the mirror pane semi-transparent and slightly reflective with soft highlight streaks, but avoid strong reflections that obscure the colored spheres.

Superposition guides appear only when showSuperposition is true in single-row mode, and should be translucent enough not to distract from the original figure geometry.

discrepancies: The mirror plane is much narrower and more edge-on than in the source, with the dark cyan edge appearing on the opposite side of the pane.
The reflected molecules are overly translucent and positioned clearly to the right of the mirror rather than appearing as crisp reflections within/behind the blue mirror surface as in the source.
The line-bond structural formulas are compressed and slightly misproportioned compared with the source, especially the hashed wedges and solid wedges.
The ball-and-stick molecules are smaller and more separated from the mirror than in the source, reducing the tight left-to-right textbook composition.
The generated figure adds interactive halos, popups, and explanatory UI elements that are not part of the original figure, though they are mostly optional.
